From Metrology to Autonomy: Why Intel Foundry’s Manufacturing Roadmap Mattersby Daniel Nenni on 10-28-2026 at 10:00 am

View Profile

View Forum Posts

View Articles

Private Message

Categories: Chiplet, Events, Intel Foundry, Semiconductor

Key takeaways ▼

Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on precise measurement. As devices become more complex and packaging integrates more components, however, measuring individual process steps is no longer enough. Manufacturers need to understand how decisions across fabrication, assembly, and test affect the finished product. Intel Foundry’s SEMICON West 2026 presentations describe an effort to build that connected intelligence, with implications for yield, quality, and factory autonomy.
Lori Scott, Intel Foundry’s senior director of business operations and marketing, recently outlined research spanning metrology, defect classification, thermal modeling, automation, and standards. The central argument is practical: autonomous manufacturing requires trustworthy measurements, connected infrastructure, and clear engineering oversight. Adding AI to disconnected systems cannot provide those foundations.
Metrology’s expanding role is especially important. Traditionally, measurements help determine whether a manufacturing step meets specifications. Connected metrology can also help engineers investigate relationships among materials, equipment conditions, contamination, and downstream defects. Earlier detection could prevent additional processing of compromised material, reducing wasted capacity and shortening investigations. Achieving that benefit requires reliable links between measurements and the production conditions that generated them.
Advanced packaging increases the stakes. Chiplets, hybrid bonding, and stacked devices bring manufacturing stages into closer technical and economic dependence. A defective component discovered after assembly can undermine the value of other components already integrated into the package. Consequently, identifying suitable die before assembly and connecting test results with manufacturing history become increasingly consequential.
Intel Foundry describes its Advanced Chiplet Test services as part of this broader measurement strategy. Capabilities including predictive die classification, intelligent die pairing, optical testing, and yield analytics are intended to inform manufacturing decisions. Their importance lies in the potential to make test information useful earlier, when engineers have more opportunities to prevent expensive downstream issues.
AI could accelerate that learning, but its authority needs boundaries. Intel Foundry’s automatic defect classification research uses an agentic workflow to assist engineers with logs, knowledge retrieval, investigations, and recipe reviews. Human approval checkpoints preserve oversight. This distinction matters because identifying a statistical association does not establish its cause or justify changing a production recipe.
For fab managers, the operational question is therefore specific: which recommendations may proceed automatically, and which require review? A useful deployment should preserve the underlying evidence, identify affected tools and lots, record uncertainty, and document approval. Otherwise, faster recommendations could simply transfer verification work to engineers while making accountability harder to establish.
Physics-informed thermal modeling offers another potentially valuable direction. Intel Foundry reports research combining AI with heat-transfer physics to improve predictions while requiring less training data. For power-dense devices and heterogeneous packages, better thermal understanding could support design, test, and reliability decisions. Production value, however, depends on validation across relevant materials, architectures, workloads, and operating conditions.
Infrastructure determines whether these capabilities scale. Data trapped inside incompatible equipment platforms limits visibility and complicates deployment across factories. Hardware-independent automation, connected systems, and edge computing could make information easier to exchange and act upon. Open standards may also reduce the integration burden when manufacturers introduce new equipment or extend automation into assembly and test.
Intel Foundry highlights SATAS, an industry consortium developing interoperable architectures and automation frameworks, as one route toward that coordination. Shared interfaces and material-handling standards matter because factory autonomy involves interactions among many suppliers. Progress requires those systems to exchange information consistently and respond predictably when conditions change.
Why does this matter? Semiconductor competitiveness depends partly on turning complex processes into repeatable, economically viable production. Connected measurement and analysis could help manufacturers learn faster, protect valuable assemblies, and use engineering resources more effectively.
The evidence presented remains a roadmap of research and emerging capabilities, rather than proof of factory-wide autonomous performance. Customers should ultimately judge success through demonstrated improvements in yield, scrap, cycle time, reliability, and engineering workload. Intel Foundry’s broader message is nevertheless significant: scalable autonomy begins with dependable evidence and coordinated systems, with explicit responsibility for every consequential manufacturing decision.
